name: openai/mle-bench
why: D4's 75 Kaggle competitions with medal grading (LICENSE file is MIT; GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Process to borrow: at least 3 seeds reported as mean and standard error, a Low-complexity "Lite" split (158 GB vs 3.3 TB), rule-break and plagiarism checks. Lesson: intake to its leaderboard paused 2026-04-24 "while we develop an improved process for ensuring submissions are fair and comparable", and ensemble rows that used test-set feedback are listed apart. Too heavy for a v0.1 task set.

name: InfiAgent/InfiAgent
why: D1's DAEval: 257 closed-form data-analysis questions over 52 CSVs with a ReAct agent in a Docker sandbox; the "@name[answer]" label format makes grading a regex match, the most reusable known-answer format for v0.1. Lesson: README logs "DAEval with human filtering updated" (2024-01-27), so labels were revised after release. README badge puts the data under CC BY-NC 4.0 (code Apache-2.0).

name: yiyihum/da-code
why: D2's 500 data-wrangling, ML and EDA tasks with a per-task evaluation config, gold files and a timeout per run. Borrow: scorers per output type (table, chart, ML prediction) rather than one generic grader. Only 100 examples ship in the repo; the full set is a separate download.

name: allenai/discoverybench
why: D6's 264 real tasks derived from published papers plus 903 synthetic tasks, with agents/ and eval/ folders (LICENSE file is ODC-By; GitHub reports NOASSERTION). Lesson from D6: include a no-data baseline (NoDataGuess) to measure how much of a published finding the model already knows; scoring uses a GPT-4 evaluator, so grader bias is a risk.

name: behavioral-data/BLADE
why: D7's 12 datasets with expert "multiverse" ground truth (variables, transformations, models chosen by independent analysts); code Apache-2.0, data ODC-By per README badge. Lesson: README says "We are working on a hold-out test set", so the public set can leak; the format scores analytic decisions, not one number, which suits open-ended questions.

name: OSU-NLP-Group/ScienceAgentBench
why: D8's 102 tasks from 44 papers. Process to borrow: Hugging Face copy holds inputs only while gold programs and eval data sit in a password-protected zip (anti-contamination), a containerised harness that runs 102 tasks in about 30 minutes on 8 threads, and a 2026-04-30 "verified" split released to fix false negatives (see D15). Data is not to be redistributed.

name: mitdbg/Kramabench
why: D10's 104 end-to-end pipeline tasks (633 sub-tasks, 1.7 GB) with reference pipelines, so intermediate steps are scored as well as the final answer. No licence detected, so do not copy. README leaderboard lists only older models (GPT-o3, Claude-3.5), so it lags the paper.

name: ucbepic/DataAgentBench
why: D11's DAB: 5 trials per query, pull-request leaderboard that requires execution traces, and SUBMISSION_RUBRIC.md leakage checks. Lessons in README footnotes: contaminated trials counted as fails (agents loaded external gold labels), a validator re-scored after a tie in the ground truth (issue 86), and rows given per-query notes or tools. Best untuned row 0.8858 vs best tuned 0.9917 (README fetched 2026-11-21; it lists 12 datasets and 54 queries, fewer than the paper). No licence detected.

name: MetaCopilot/dseval
why: D5's DSEval toolkit and four problem sets (Exercise, SO, LeetCode, Kaggle; 187, 202, 40, 396 problems per README) with validators that go beyond correctness, e.g. an "intact" check that the agent did not alter the input data. Borrow the silent-data-mutation validator. Stale since 2024-06.

name: LiqiangJing/DSBench
why: D3's 466 analysis and 74 modelling tasks from ModelOff and Kaggle (LICENSE file is MIT; GitHub reports NOASSERTION). README says OpenAI used it to evaluate its ChatGPT agent (2025-07). Lesson from D3: answers are judged by a GPT-4o semantic-match function, and humans score only 64% on the 10 sampled competitions, so ceiling and label noise matter.

name: xxxiaol/QRData
why: D14's 411 statistics and causal questions with gold answers in benchmark/QRData.json plus eval.py (3 percent numeric tolerance); built from textbook and paper data, a candidate known-answer set. Lesson: README strikes out the sister QRText set because "some numerical questions ... encounter measurement errors" in the gold answers. LICENSE file is CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial), so check before reuse.

name: XinmingTu/BenchGuard
why: D15's benchmark auditor, shipped as a Claude Code plugin (/benchguard-skill:audit-benchmark) that cross-checks the instruction, reference solution, grader and environment (LICENSE file is Apache-2.0). README: findings are "a queue for a human expert to check, not final judgments". Borrow: audit our own known-answer tasks before any study, and a worked example of a marketplace plugin.

name: uiuc-kang-lab/ELT-Bench
why: The data-engineering benchmark audited in D13; README links REPRODUCE.md with the commands for every experiment and mentions mutation operators and analysis programs. Needs Docker, Airbyte and Snowflake, so heavy. No licence detected by GitHub (README badge says CC BY-SA 4.0).

name: WecoAI/aideml
why: AIDE, the draft-debug-improve tree-search scaffold behind the D4 baselines (o1-preview 16.9%). README separates the algorithm, this lean research repo and a commercial product. Lesson from the MLE-bench README leaderboard: later systems list 60%+ while AIDE with o1-preview is listed at 17.12%, so the scaffold matters as much as the model.

name: huggingface/smolagents
why: Code-writing agent library; its "smolagents DR" variant is the strongest baseline in D10 (55.83% overall vs 24.98% for the best fixed pipeline, Section 4) and in D12. Lesson from D12: silent errors persist even in DS-STAR, an agent that already iterates with verification, so an agent loop alone is not a correctness check.

name: google-research/era
why: Google Research's ERA (paper by Aygun et al. 2025, arXiv:2509.06503, catalogued in folder 06): tree search over LLM-written code against a scorable task (scRNA-seq batch integration, Kaggle Playground). Borrow: score-driven search needs a task with a numeric score, and the repo shows how that scorer is wired. Apache-2.0.

name: kenqgu/RADAR
why: RADAR (D17, Google Research / UW): programmatic injection of missing values, outliers and logical inconsistencies into real tables, with 260 query-specific perturbation functions. Borrow: perturb a known-answer dataset so a naive computation gives a wrong answer, a cheap silent-error test for our analysis agent. Apache-2.0; dataset licences listed per dataset in the paper appendix.

name: MMTU-Benchmark/MMTU
why: MMTU (D18, Microsoft and U. Michigan): 28,000+ table questions over 25 tasks with automatic graders (NeurIPS 2025). Lesson: even GPT-5 scores about 69.6% on expert table tasks (join, cleaning, transformation); table skills are a floor under any analysis agent. No licence detected by GitHub, so read-only.

name: Future-House/BixBench
why: FutureHouse's BixBench (D19): Jupyter-notebook analysis capsules with open-answer and multiple-choice grading, plus a custom agent harness. Borrow: the refusal option and the open-answer versus multiple-choice split, which show MCQ scores can be near chance. Apache-2.0 code; data on Hugging Face.

name: benjamin-kohler/social_science_replicability
why: ETH Zurich code for D22: extract methods from a paper, run the agent with information isolation (no original code or results), compare cell by cell, attribute root causes. Borrow: cell-level comparison against published numbers as a known-answer grader for an economics-style study. No licence detected, so read-only.

name: uiuc-kang-lab/REPRO-Bench
why: REPRO-Bench (Hu et al. 2025, UIUC, arXiv:2507.18901, catalogued in folder 06): 112 social-science papers with reproduction packages and public reproduction reports; the best agent scored 21.4%, below random guessing among four options. A critical result for any claim that agents can audit a study. No licence detected, so read-only.

name: trl-lab/ds-agent-failures
why: Test suite from D23 (CWI): six controlled tests for data leakage and bad validation in agent-written pipelines, plus a failure-mode taxonomy. Borrow: leakage checks (imputing or scaling before the split, ignoring time order) as a gate on the kit's modelling output. MIT.

name: zjunlp/DataMind
why: Zhejiang University data-analysis agent repo; it is the only GitHub link on D24's first page (LongDS-Bench: 68 multi-turn tasks from Kaggle notebooks, 2,225 turns, state update, rollback and counterfactual patterns), and D21 cites DataMind as an agent trained for data analysis. Not verified to hold the LongDS tasks; check its README before use. No licence detected, so read-only.

name: AMA-CMFAI/DSAEval
why: DSAEval (D25, PolyU): 641 data-science problems over 285 datasets run in a Jupyter-kernel sandbox, scored by two LLM judges on reasoning, code and results. Lesson: judge scoring was calibrated against three PhD annotators; useful when no single right answer exists, weaker than known answers. No licence detected, so read-only.

name: vis-nlp/DSAgentBench
why: DSAgentBench (D27, York U. VIS-NLP lab): 275 end-to-end data-science workflow tasks on an OSWorld-based desktop (Jupyter, VS Code, terminal, browser), each with a deterministic Python evaluator for analytical correctness, visual output and model performance. Borrow: execution-based checkers instead of an LLM judge, and a real-computer harness comparable to the kit's computer-use walk design. Apache-2.0.

name: microsoft/RD-Agent
why: R&D-Agent from D28: an MLE-bench agent split into two phases and six components; MIT-licensed and widely starred, but stars are not evidence. Read its component split when designing the study factory's data-science agents
